html:
The first factory to make sugar from beet, opened in 1801 at Cunern (now Konary) in Silesia, then part of Prussia. It was built by the chemist Franz Karl Achard with money from the Prussian king.

Until then Europe's sugar came from cane grown in the Caribbean and Brazil by enslaved Africans, a trade at the heart of the Atlantic slave trade. In 1747 the Berlin chemist Andreas Marggraf had found that beet root holds the same sugar as cane. Achard, his student, bred beets with more sugar and worked out how to extract it on a large scale.

The breakthrough came in war. When Britain blockaded Europe and Napoleon closed the continent to British trade, cane sugar became scarce, and Napoleon pushed beet growing and factories in France from 1811. After his fall cheap cane came back and many factories closed, but the industry recovered.

Beet let temperate Europe grow its own sugar and helped make sugar a cheap everyday food, as crystal sugar had once been a luxury.
